newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Royal Opera gala staged after bomb scare.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Royal Opera gala staged after bomb scare.

text.p: Britain's Royal Opera company on Thursday celebrated its 50th anniversary in dramatic fashion with a glittering gala delayed 30 minutes by a bomb scare.

Heir to the throne Prince Charles, guest of honour at the gala, was brought in through a side entrance at the Covent Garden theatre while musicians and opera fans in their evening finery were kept behind security cordons.
But police said a suspect package spotted in the street outside turned out to be harmless and the performance was given the all-clear.
Star of the evening was Spanish tenor Placido Domingo who was celebrating 25 years of appearances with one of the world's most famous opera companies.
He warned fans who had paid up to 1,000 pounds ($1,650) a seat that he was suffering from the start of a cold, but they still gave him a rousing reception.
The stars all gave their services free for the gala celebration where devotees of the Opera House were all treated to free champagne in the interval.
"In spite of security scares and sore throats, you have given us a wonderful performance," Chief Opera House fundraiser Vivien Duffield said.
The Royal Opera House is to close next July for two years of much-needed renovation to its dilapidated backstage facilities.

The National Lottery has contributed almost 80 million pounds ($130 million) to the rebuilding work but the Opera House is now looking for another 100 million pounds ($165 million) from private sponsors.

Domingo was in nostalgic form, recalling: "Twenty-five years ago, I made my debut as Cavaradossi in Tosca. Many roles later, Covent Garden remains for me one of the most exciting and rewarding places to perform."

Domingo, whose velvety voice and flawless technique have made him one of the world's most sought-after performers, said: "The Royal Opera House audience loves tradition, is hugely knowledgeable and yet very warm."
Pitching in behind the Opera House fundraisers, he said: "It deserves to have its theatre refurbished."
Organisers confidently expect the gala, which was carried live on British and Japanese television, will raise more than 500,000 pounds ($800,000).
Exactly 50 years ago, the Royal Opera House company took part with Sadler's Wells ballet in a production of Henry Purcell's Fairy Queen.
That was recalled on Thursday when excerpts from Purcell were played once more beneath the elegant chandeliers and balconies bedecked in Christmas lights.
Among the other big attractions at the gala were soprano Angela Gheorgiu and Roberto Alagna, the new "golden couple" of opera, who sang a duet from Bizet's Carmen.
The company's 50 years have been dotted with many memorable highlights from the rise of Australian soprano Joan Sutherland to the premier of Benjamin Britten's Billy Budd.
But there have been boos along with the cheers.

Richard Jones' controversial production of "Das Rheingold" provoked outrage among the traditionalists while Marilyn Horne once invited one booing operagoer to come up on stage and "sort it out kinda man-to-man".
